rv.q: One only wishes that the score were less generic – a second-act duet between Barrie and Sylvia is especially vapid – and that the writing were as piquant as the stagecraft.
Finding Neverland is still too treacly — it lacks the edge and humor of both Wicked and Matilda — and the tear-wringing ending just goes on forever.

The musical, which opened Wednesday at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre, is a sweet if predictable entertainment that transforms the story of how J.M. Barrie came to write 'Peter Pan' into a family-friendly spectacle.
It's a celebration of imagination that labors hard for a consistent tone and often leaves you feeling manipulated.
"Finding Neverland" still needs to find itself.
No matter how many emotionally effective touches the actors and their director provide, the evening keeps returning to those mostly forgettable tunes.

When the brightest element in Diane Paulus's tacky staging is Kelsey Grammer as a curmudgeonly producer, you know it's time to get the hook.
When that inner child is there from the start — to the extent it's ever there at all, within Morrison — it means that the actual finding in "Finding Neverland" never feels logical.

But there’s no disguising the feeling that almost every element of the production has a secondhand, synthetic quality: the dialogue, the jerky choreography (by Mia Michaels), the jokes, the anachronistic depiction of the show people who put on Barrie’s plays.
The result is a well-intentioned muddle, though it does offer the best use of stage glitter since Hedwig’s eye makeup.
Show-doctored into a state of shrill mediocrity, the patient can barely walk, let alone fly.

Bombastic and exhausting, the show confuses childishness with an affinity for the child inside, at times recalling Wicked in its busily assaultive hyperactivity, but without that show’s catchy songs or engaging central character dynamic.

The moments of pixie-dusted perfection come from Paulus' mind—especially one visually breathtaking moment of swirling, sparkled sadness.

"“Finding Neverland” is a thoroughly enchanting new musical. Diane Paulus, the show’s current director, has kept this musical tale about J. M. Barrie’s creation of “Peter Pan” magnificently low tech...she creates magic not by being literal but recalling stage machinery that’s appropriate to the year of Barrie’s classic play, 1904...
I found it well cast, funny, touching, and well developed.

The end result is both rousing and erratic, with bits of thrilling stage magic that are signature Diane Paulus (she also directed “Pippin” and “Hair”), and dialogue that sometimes feels as if it’s been focus group-sanitized to within an inch of its life.
But Paulus' staging can — and does — go overboard.
But the work fails to live up to the story's promise.

While the show has been guided by the brilliant film mogul Harvey Weinstein and directed with care, intelligence, and a few flourishes of genuine theatrical magic by Tony Award winner Diane Paulus, it never really takes flight or finds its true voice.
Finding Neverland turns out to be the three hankie show of the season with a lump in its throat and a tear in the eye.
Finding Neverland is an enjoyable musical, from start to finish.
For a show that should be about the inexplicable magic of creation, every scene in James Graham’s book seems overwritten.
Finding Neverland, a show that should have enchanted but, instead, disappoints.

In the end, the hero and savior of this musical is Harvey Weinstein, for if it wasn’t for his dogged persistence, the theater would have lost a lovely score, a hammy Kelsey Grammer, a yummy Matthew Morrison, and a fun, familiar family show.

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet this family-friendly musical about J.M. Barrie creating Peter Pan. Critics praise Matthew Morrison's charming performance and visual spectacle, but fault the show for being manipulative, overstuffed, and relying too heavily on nostalgia.

sg.ra: Per SeatPlan and Headout, center rows D-J are the Lunt-Fontanne sweet spot because the house stage sits unusually high and is not raked — patrons halfway back in orchestra report they cannot see the stage floor, so anchoring forward of the overhang line (row W) but back from rows A-C keeps the stage floor visible.

Front Mezz is only 5 rows deep (A-E) with no balcony above, so every row has clean sightlines — and row B specifically beats row A because a safety railing in front of row A cuts into the stage (one source cites ~35% obstruction for some seats), making B the preferred pick that most guides name by row.

SeatPlan and forum posts flag that the mezzanine overhang starts at row J but begins cutting into the top of the stage from row W back across Left, Center, and Right Orchestra — combined with the Lunt-Fontanne's high unraked stage (floor already hard to see from mid-orchestra), rear orchestra loses both the top and bottom of the picture.

The Lunt-Fontanne has no balcony, so unlike most large Nederlander houses the Rear Mezz has zero overhang — SeatPlan specifically names rows B-C as best because they clear the railing behind the Front Mezz that can obstruct row A, and the section's rake keeps sightlines clean despite being the cheapest seats in the venue.

Multiple guides flag that the Lunt-Fontanne's unusually high, non-raked stage makes rows A-C worse than typical Broadway front rows — Headout and TickPick-linked guides warn sightlines can be obstructed because the stage is raised, and any tall patron in front blocks center-stage action at this proximity.
